did_you_know.text: Zelophehad's daughters showed great courage by standing before the entire leadership, including Moses and Eleazar, to demand their rights, an unprecedented act for women at that time.

The main motivation of Zelophehad's daughters was to prevent 'the diminishing of our father's name,' meaning to preserve their father's family name and his share of the inheritance, even though he had no sons.

The case of Zelophehad's daughters is a rare example in the Torah where a new law or significant legal instruction was established following a plea from citizens, demonstrating the flexibility of divine law.
The reason for Moses being barred from entering the Land of Israel is mentioned again here: 'the waters of Meribah Kadesh,' where he struck the rock instead of speaking to it as commanded by God.

When Moses prays for a leader, he addresses God with the unique title: 'God of the spirits of all flesh,' emphasizing God's ability to know the soul of every person and choose the most suitable leader.
The imagery of the people of Israel as 'sheep without a shepherd' emphasizes the leader's importance in ancient Near Eastern culture, whose role was to protect, guide, and care for the flock.
The phrase 'a man in whom is spirit,' describing Joshua, can be interpreted as someone possessing a spirit of prophecy, wisdom, or special natural leadership talents.
Unlike Moses, who spoke directly with God, Joshua would receive divine guidance through the 'judgment of the Urim' performed by Eleazar the priest, which changed the nature of spiritual leadership.
